# How Suspense works

Suspense is an application for working on a project whose spec, written in Piton, describes its code. The user sends you prompts from it in one of five modes:

- Code changes the code and leaves the spec as it is.
- Chain changes the spec, then the code to match it.
- Spec changes the spec and leaves the code as it is.
- Ask asks a question and changes nothing.
- Freeform passes a prompt to you exactly as typed.

Code, Chain, Spec, and Freeform prompts are tasks. Tasks run in two lanes, a spec lane and a code lane, one task at a time in each; a task waits in the queue behind the tasks of its own lane. Questions from Ask run at once and never queue.

A Chain prompt runs as two steps, each its own run in its own lane. The spec step writes the prompt into the spec. Once the spec is built, the code step is sent the same prompt and what the spec step replied, and changes the code to match the spec as built.

Suspense adds each mode's instructions to a prompt itself, in a block marked <task-instructions> at its head, together with the spec's references and the task's understanding file. So a prompt written for a mode is only what the user wants done, in the user's own terms. Never put a <task-instructions> block in a prompt you write, nor steps the mode already takes, nor instructions about building, checking, or the understanding file.

To write a good prompt for each mode:

- A Chain or Spec prompt says what should be true of the application once it is met, not how to edit the spec.
- A Code prompt says what the code should do, and may link to the compiled reference for the part of the spec it follows.
- An Ask prompt is a question.
- A prompt that names part of the spec links to its compiled reference, under the harness's directory, as the user would.

# How Suspense works

Suspense is an application for working on a project whose spec, written in Piton, describes its code. The user sends you prompts from it in one of five modes:

- Code changes the code and leaves the spec as it is.
- Chain changes the spec, then the code to match it.
- Spec changes the spec and leaves the code as it is.
- Ask asks a question and changes nothing.
- Freeform passes a prompt to you exactly as typed.

Code, Chain, Spec, and Freeform prompts are tasks. Tasks run in two lanes, a spec lane and a code lane, one task at a time in each; a task waits in the queue behind the tasks of its own lane. Questions from Ask run at once and never queue.

A Chain prompt runs as two steps, each its own run in its own lane. The spec step writes the prompt into the spec. Once the spec is built, the code step is sent the same prompt and what the spec step replied, and changes the code to match the spec as built.

Suspense adds each mode's instructions to a prompt itself, in a block marked <task-instructions> at its head, together with the spec's references and the task's understanding file. So a prompt written for a mode is only what the user wants done, in the user's own terms. Never put a <task-instructions> block in a prompt you write, nor steps the mode already takes, nor instructions about building, checking, or the understanding file.

To write a good prompt for each mode:

- A Chain or Spec prompt says what should be true of the application once it is met, not how to edit the spec.
- A Code prompt says what the code should do, and may link to the compiled reference for the part of the spec it follows.
- An Ask prompt is a question.
- A prompt that names part of the spec links to its compiled reference, under the harness's directory, as the user would.

An answer hands a prompt back to the user as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-prompt` and the mode it is for, such as ```` ```suspense-prompt chain ````, holding only the prompt's text. It asks the user something back as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-question`: the question first, then any answers to pick from, one per line, each starting with `- `. Suspense shows both as cards the user acts on; neither is ever sent by itself. A prompt card has buttons that send it to Code, Chain, or Spec, whichever mode it names, and one that puts it in the chat input to edit first.

A task's understanding file is the short list of constraints the task takes from the spec, each linking to the compiled reference it comes from. Suspense shows it beside the task as it runs.

The user can cancel a task, resend it, send it to the other mode, send more to a task while it runs, and start a new conversation. A prompt never needs to say that any of this is possible.
----
This project is written in Piton, a declarative language for agent guidance.

- Source of truth: the `.pi` files under `./spec`. Compiled Markdown is derived output.
- Make lasting changes in the Piton source, then run `piton build`; never hand-edit generated artifacts.
- Compiled reference documents live under `.claude/reference`. Links between them are lazy: follow one when the work touches what it describes.
- Scoped guidance is written to `CLAUDE.md` files placed next to the code they describe.
- `piton check` validates the specbase; `piton reach` shows what the entrypoints can see; `piton slice file.pi#Anchor.property` prints just the spec one thing depends on.

# Piton Fluency

This is a working reference for Piton, the Belay framework bundled with it, the
project configuration, the package manager and the tooling. Read it before you
read or change a Piton specbase. It is generated from the specification in
`spec/` by the GenerateFluencyPrompt skill. Where the compiler behaves
differently from the spec, the text below says so, and section 16 lists every
known gap.

## 1. What Piton is, and why

Piton is a declarative, whitespace-structured language for writing agent
guidance: skills, agents, commands, scoped instructions and reference
documents. Its author calls it a "semi-natural programming language". Prose and
structure are both first-class. A value can be a paragraph of plain English or
a typed, inherited, composed data structure, and most files mix the two.

The founding thesis (`spec/scope/founding-thesis/`) explains the design:

- Every programming language is an abstraction over the layer beneath it. Once
  an abstraction is accepted, nobody cares how its compiled output is produced,
  as long as the output is good. Agentic development is the next step in that
  history. In this model the agent is the compiler.
- Humans are good at designing coherent systems, not at typing out the latest
  accepted abstraction. Piton keeps the describing, constraining and thinking,
  and hands the manual labour to the agent.
- Prompting an agent session by session produces results that live in one
  developer's memory and cannot be traced. AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and Markdown
  skills help, but pure prose decays. It is ambiguous, it gets duplicated, and
  it has no tools for reuse. Piton adds imports, inheritance, types and
  references to prose, while keeping prose for the things prose says best
  ("the button should be blue with contrasting text"). Plain prompting is fine
  for a small one-off tool. A sufficiently complex system needs a traceable
  artifact of the process itself, not just its output, and more so when
  several people work on it.
- The real problem is repetition. Much software work is the same patterns
  again (CRUD APIs, layouts, navigation bars, modal forms). Functions, classes
  and generics are ways of wrapping a problem once it becomes a pattern. The
  aim is to keep designing systems and stop typing the patterns: "I never
  wanted to write code itself; I wanted to create."
- The CNC analogy: G-code replaced the machinist's hand, and CAM then sat on
  top of G-code by combining design intent with the machinist's expertise. The
  CAM engineer never types G-code but is essential. CNC did not replace most of
  the machinist's skill, and two jobs (engineer, machinist) became three (plus
  the CAM engineer). The Piton author plays that role for agents.
- The stated goal is that you can paste the specification into an agentic
  coding tool and get a compiler for Piton and Belay back. This repository is
  that experiment. The specification in `spec/` is written in Piton, and the
  compiler in `crates/` is judged against it.

Core facts:

- **There is no runtime.** Piton compiles to data (JSON, YAML, Markdown)
  through **renderers**. Frameworks such as Belay add **adapters** on top of
  the renderers. There are no functions, no loops, and no conditionals except
  the ternary operator. Every value is immutable.
- **The `.pi` source is the source of truth.** Compiled Markdown under
  `.claude/reference`, `.claude/skills`, `CLAUDE.md` files and so on is derived
  output. Make lasting changes in the `.pi` files and rebuild. Never hand-edit
  generated artifacts.
- A **specbase** is a Piton project: a `piton.config.pi`, a source root
  (usually `spec/`), an entry file, and the frameworks and packages it uses.
- **Successful compilation shows that the guidance is well-formed. It does not
  show that an agent will behave correctly.** Artifact generation is
  predictable, but agent behaviour is probabilistic.

## 2. Files, whitespace, comments, keywords

- Source files use the `.pi` extension. A directory that contains an
  `index.pi` is a module (section 7.2).
- **Indentation defines structure**, as in Python. Tabs or any number of
  spaces are accepted, but one file must be consistent. The canonical style is
  4 spaces. `piton format` enforces it, and it cannot be configured.
- **Comments** are line-only and start with `//`. There are no block comments.
  **A comment has to be on its own line.** After code, `//` is just text, so
  `url: https://example.com // note` is the string
  `https://example.com // note`. The formatter adds one space after `//` when
  there is none and touches nothing else in the comment, so commented-out code
  keeps its spacing. To start a value with `//`, escape it:
  `\ // \ Just Text`.
- **Reserved words** have special meaning:

  ```
  anchor abstract export from import use as extends pass
  this self super
  true false null
  any simple complex
  string number boolean list dictionary
  ```

  You can't use them as your own keywords (`reserved-keyword`), but **you can
  use them as keys**. As keys they are just strings: `null: text`,
  `use: text` and `as: text` are ordinary properties.
- **Keywords** are all lowercase and may be kebab-case
  (`arithmetic-operator`). Users define their own with `as` (section 8.6).
- **`pass`** fills the body of an anchor that has no properties of its own. An
  anchor always needs something indented under it; `anchor X:` with nothing
  under it is `empty-anchor`.

  ```piton
  anchor Child extends Base:
      pass
  ```

## 3. Declarations and values

A file is a sequence of top-level declarations. Top-level names are variables
scoped to their file: they are global within the file and invisible outside it
unless exported.

```piton
myVariable: 42
export pi: 3.14

export anchor MyAnchor:
    description: This is my anchor
```

`key: value` assigns a value, and the space after the colon is required. The
value can sit on the same line or be indented on the lines below:

```piton
sameLine: Hello, World!
nextLine:
    Hello, World!
```

Both produce `"Hello, World!"`. The leading indentation belongs to the syntax,
not to the string.

**A property has to have a value.** A name with nothing after it and nothing
indented under it is a compiler error (`empty-value`). If you mean nothing,
write `null`. The one exception is a required property in an abstract anchor
(`title:: string`); anywhere else a constraint with no value is
`missing-value`.

### 3.1 Types

Piton is loosely typed, with optional constraints.

| Type | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `string` | Unicode text. Never quoted (section 3.3). |
| `number` | One numeric type, a 64-bit IEEE 754 float, with no int/float distinction. |
| `boolean` | Lowercase `true` and `false`. |
| `null` | Lowercase `null`. It is the only "nothing" value (there is no `undefined`), and `{null == null}` is `true`. |
| `list` | An ordered collection. Item types may be mixed unless a constraint says otherwise. |
| `dictionary` | Key/value pairs. Keys are strings, and value types may be mixed unless constrained. |
| anchor | The one user-defined type (section 8). |

- **Simple types** are string, number, boolean and null.
- **Complex types** are list, dictionary and anchor.
- A **reference** is its own type, produced by `@{}` (section 6.5). It points
  at an anchor or a property on one instead of copying it.

- **Inference.** An unconstrained variable or property can hold any type,
  inferred from how the value looks: `true` is a boolean but `true story` is
  a string; `42` and `-42` are numbers but `42 things` is a string; `A + B`
  and `This costs $5 + tax` are strings (no braces, no expression); `null` is
  null; `"false"` is a string; `${a + b}` is always a string.

Every built-in type is described by an anchor that uses the abstract `type`
keyword (`spec/scope/language/types/lib/Type.pi`). A `type` anchor provides a
`description` (simple or complex) and its `supportedOperators` (a list of
operators, or null). Using an operator a type does not list is a compiler
error, but the compiler applies the coercion (4.2) and inference rules before
it reports one:

| Type | Supported operators |
| --- | --- |
| number | arithmetic `+ - * / %`, comparison `== != < <= > >=` |
| string | concatenation `+`, `++`, comparison `== != < <= > >=` |
| boolean | logical `&& \|\| !`, `==`, `!=` |
| null | `==`, `!=` |
| list | merge `+`, `++`, `==`, `!=` |
| dictionary | `.`, merge `+`, `++`, `==`, `!=` |
| anchor | `.`, `==`, `!=` |
| reference | `==`, `!=` |

### 3.2 Numbers

```piton
myInt: 123
myFloat: 3.14
mySmallFloat: 0.14
myBigNumber: 1_200_000.00
negative: -5
```

- **A decimal needs its leading `0`.** `0.14` is a number; `.5` is not a number
  (unconstrained, it is the string `".5"`).
- `_` may separate digits for readability.
- **There is no exponent notation.** `1e3` is not a number (unconstrained, it
  is silently the string `"1e3"`, not an error).
- A negative number is written with a minus, like `-5`. A list item always has
  a space after its dash, so `-5` is a number and `- 5` is a list item.
- **The minus is only part of a number.** There's no minus in front of an
  expression: `{-price}` is an error. Write `{0 - price}`.
- Compiled numbers take their shortest form: `1_200_000.00` becomes `1200000`
  and `0.50` becomes `0.5`.

### 3.3 Strings and quotes

- Strings are not quoted. **Quotes are ordinary characters in a value**, so
  `greeting: "Hello"` is the string `"Hello"`, quotes and all, and
  `"false"` is a string with quotes in it, never a boolean.
- The one exception is inside an expression, where bare words are symbols, so
  string operands are written in double quotes: `{"Hello" + name}`. There the
  quotes are not part of the string.
- In a multi-line block, consecutive lines join with one space. **A blank line
  starts a new paragraph**, which compiles to a line break (`\n`). Several
  blank lines in a row still count as one.

  ```piton
  myString:
      This broken string is not considered
      a line break.

      While this *is* a new paragraph because there was a blank line above.
  ```

  This compiles to
  `"This broken string is not considered a line break.\nWhile this *is* a new paragraph because there was a blank line above."`.

- **Markdown in a string is plain text.** Piton has no link syntax, so
  `[the guide](./guide.md)` and `![A diagram](./diagram.png)` pass through
  exactly as written. Nothing resolves, rewrites or checks them, and they are
  never an error. The only links Piton makes are `@{}` references.

### 3.4 Escaping

Escaping works by wrapping. Put backslashes around the special characters,
with a space on each side. The spaces are part of the wrapper and are removed:
`\ {1 + 2 + 3} \` compiles to the literal `{1 + 2 + 3}`. It is the only way to
escape, and even a single character gets wrapped: `\ : \` gives `:`.

- **Stacking.** To escape backslashes themselves, use more of them. The
  closing wrapper must match the opening one, so anything inside can use fewer:
  `\\ \ {x} \ \\` compiles to `\ {x} \`.
- **Multi-line escape blocks.** A line holding only backslashes opens a block,
  and a line with the same number of backslashes closes it. Everything in
  between is kept exactly, line breaks and indentation included. The spec uses
  three backslashes (`\\\`) for these.
- **Code fences are ordinary text.** A ```` ``` ```` fence does not protect
  anything: expressions, comments, list items and keys inside it are still
  parsed. So put an escape block inside the fence, the way every example in the
  spec does:

  ````piton
  description:
      ```piton
      \\\
      anchor Example:
          value: {1 + 2}
      \\\
      ```
  ````

  This keeps the fence and the example exactly as written. Markdown tables
  need the same treatment, because otherwise their rows join into one line.

**Prose pitfalls.** Each of these silently changes the structure of a string
block:

- A line that starts `- ` makes a list item, and a line that starts `+ ` or
  `++ ` makes a composition line (section 5). A property declared `:: string`
  then fails. Escape the start: `\ - \ item`.
- A line shaped like `word: text` (`Similarly: ...`, `Inputs: none`, or a
  wrapped line that happens to start with `type:`) becomes a dictionary key,
  and the block turns into an implicit list. Escape the colon (`\ : \`) or
  rewrap the paragraph.
- Backticks do not protect anything. `` `{x}` `` is still an expression, and
  `` `a + b` `` in a table cell is text only because it has no braces.
- An expression in running text changes the value's shape when it evaluates
  to a list, dictionary or anchor (section 6.2).

Wrapping stops text being parsed as syntax, but it doesn't change the inferred
type: `\ false \` is still the boolean `false`. To get the string, write
`${false}`.

The wrapper is the only way to escape. A backslash that doesn't open a
wrapper (a backslash followed by a space) is just a backslash, so `\:` is the
two characters `\:`. Write `\ : \` to escape a colon.

### 3.5 Lists

```piton
markdownStyle:
    - One
    - List
    - Item

inlineStyle: [This, is, a, list, of, strings]

nestedMarkdownList:
    - Level 1
        - Level 2
            - Level 3
```

`nestedMarkdownList` is `[Level 1, [Level 2, [Level 3]]]`.

- **Items cannot be accessed by index.** By design there is no `myList[0]`.
  Piton describes things; it does not compute them, and lists exist to be
  merged and inherited.
- **A list item is never a key**, even with a colon at the end. `- Settings:`
  is just the string `"Settings:"`.
- **Anything indented under a list item is not part of that item.** It becomes
  the next item in the list, so a dictionary indented under an item is its own
  item, right after it:

  ```piton
  repos:
      - https://github.com/piton-lang/piton-rs
          tag: v1
      - https://github.com/piton-lang/other
  ```

  This compiles to
  `["https://github.com/piton-lang/piton-rs", {"tag": "v1"}, "https://github.com/piton-lang/other"]`.
  A dictionary that ends up as an item of an explicit list cannot be addressed.

### 3.6 Dictionaries

A dictionary has one syntax, which is indentation:

```piton
firstLevel:
    secondLevel:
        thirdLevel: This is a string
```

- Dot access works: `{firstLevel.secondLevel.thirdLevel}` gives
  `"This is a string"`.
- **Valid keys** contain Unicode letters, Unicode digits, `_` and `-`, and
  nothing else (no spaces, no dots). Keys are always strings, even when they
  look like something else, so `thisIsAKey`, `123`, `foo-bar`, `false` and
  `null` are valid keys, while `This is a key` and `a.b` are not.
- **A hyphen inside a name is part of the name.** `{config.foo-bar}` reads the
  key `foo-bar`. For subtraction, put spaces around the minus: `{a - b}`.
- A list indented under a key is that key's value. If the key also has
  something above the list, like text or another dictionary, the value becomes
  an implicit list (3.7) and the list goes in as one item:

  ```piton
  plain:
      - x
      - y
  mixed:
      text
      - x
      - y
  ```

  `plain` is `["x", "y"]`; `mixed` is `["text", ["x", "y"]]`.

### 3.7 Implicit lists

A block that mixes prose, list items and keys becomes an **implicit list**
that keeps the source order:

```piton
combined:
    This is a string

    - This
    - Is
    - A
    - List

    nestedDictionary:
        deeplyNestedDictionary: This is a string
```

This compiles to
`["This is a string", ["This", "Is", "A", "List"], {"nestedDictionary": {"deeplyNestedDictionary": "This is a string"}}]`.

- **Keys declared directly in the mixed block stay addressable.**
  `{combined.nestedDictionary.deeplyNestedDictionary}` still resolves.
- The prose and list elements cannot be addressed, because there is no list
  access.
- An expression in running text that gives a list, dictionary or anchor also
  makes an implicit list (section 6.2).

## 4. Variables and type constraints

- A variable is declared by naming it at the top level of a file:
  `myVariable: 42`.
- The file is its scope. `export` makes it visible to other files.
- **Inside an expression, a plain name always means a variable from the file
  (or something imported), even inside an anchor.** To reach a property on the
  anchor you are in, use `this` or `self`:

  ```piton
  x: top-level

  anchor Card:
      x: card
      fromFile: {x}
      fromCard: {this.x}
  ```

  `Card.fromFile` is `"top-level"` and `Card.fromCard` is `"card"`.
- Everything is immutable. There is no compile-time mutability.

### 4.1 Constraint syntax

A constraint is written `name:: type: value`. **The whitespace after `::` and
after `:` is mandatory**, so `myVariable::number:42` is an error
(`constraint-spacing`), in blocks as well as at the top level.

```piton
count:: number: 42
tags:: string[]: [foo, bar, baz]
config:: dictionary:
    a:: number: 1
    b:: string: foo
a:: complex: [1, 2, 3]
c:: simple: 1
g:: any: 1
h:: any:
    - String
    - [1, 2, 3]
```

- `simple` accepts string, number, boolean or null. `complex` accepts list,
  dictionary or anchor. `any` accepts anything.
- `T[]` is a list of `T`, for any type, including anchor types (`Foo[]`).
- `extends Foo[]` (or `extends Foo`) accepts anything that inherits from the
  anchor `Foo` (section 8.4). You can use it anywhere, but it is most at home
  in abstracts. The spec also uses it on exported lists:
  `export ARITHMETIC_OPERATORS:: extends ArithmeticOperator[]: ...`.
- An anchor-typed constraint (`f:: Foo: {Foo}`) is satisfied by the anchor or a
  copy of it (section 6.1).
- A file that names an abstract as a type must import it with
  `from ./Foo import Foo`. `use` alone is not enough (section 7.3).

### 4.2 Multiple constraints and coercion

Coercion is intentionally limited. With several constraints, they are tried
**left to right** and the first type the value can validly represent wins.

```piton
first:: number:: string: 42
second:: string:: number: 42
written:: string: 1.0
evaluated:: string: {1.0}
quoted:: boolean:: number:: string: "false"
```

- `first` is the number `42`; `second` is the string `"42"`.
- **A literal keeps its text when coerced to a string.** `written` is
  `"1.0"`. An expression is evaluated first and its result is coerced, so
  `evaluated` is `"1"`.
- `quoted` is the string `"false"`, quotes and all, because quotes are
  ordinary characters and `"false"` is not a boolean.
- **Booleans and null are never coerced**, to strings or anything else. `flag:: string: false`
  is a compiler error (`type-mismatch`), not the string `"false"`. If you want
  the string, write `${false}`.
- Lists, dictionaries and anchors are never coerced into unrelated types.
- If no constraint accepts the value, compilation fails with `type-mismatch`.
- These rules are about constraints. Operators such as `+` have their own
  rules (section 6.4).

### 4.3 Required and optional properties

In an abstract anchor:

```piton
abstract anchor Card:
    title:: string
    subtitle:: string:: null
    footer:: string:: null: null

anchor MyCard extends Card:
    title: Hello
    subtitle: null
```

- A constraint with no value is **required**. Anything that extends the anchor
  has to give it a value (`unimplemented-property` otherwise). Adding `null` to
  the constraint lets that value be null, but it still has to be written, so
  `title` and `subtitle` are required.
- A property with a default value is **optional**. The usual way to write one
  is to allow null and default to null, like `footer`. `x:: string:: null: null`
  gives `null`. The language server does not complain about a missing
  optional property.
- **A child can't redeclare a constraint it inherits**, only give it a value.
  If `subtitle` is already constrained, `subtitle: Hi` is fine and
  `subtitle:: string: Hi` is `redeclared-constraint`.

## 5. Composition lines inside blocks

**Blocks are built from top to bottom. A line that starts with `+` or `++`
takes everything above it and combines it with that line's value**, using the
operator of the same name (section 6.4).

```piton
anchor BaseAnchor:
    items:
        - A
        - B
        - C

anchor ChildAnchor extends BaseAnchor:
    items:
        + {super.items}
        - D
        - E
        - F
```

`ChildAnchor.items` is `[A, B, C, D, E, F]`: the block starts empty, the `+`
brings in `super.items`, then D, E and F are added. Without the `+`
(`- {super.items}`) the result is `[[A, B, C], D, E, F]`.

- On lists, `+` merges and **removes duplicates, keeping the last
  occurrence**. Items `A, B, C, D` followed by `+ {super.items}` give
  `[D, A, B, C]`.
- On lists, `++` keeps everything: items `A, B, C, D` followed by
  `++ {super.items}` give `[A, B, C, D, A, B, C]`.
- On dictionaries, `+` is a shallow merge and `++` a deep merge.
- **On strings, `+` joins with nothing in between and `++` joins with a line
  break:**

  ```piton
  anchor Base:
      d: Base text.

  anchor Plus extends Base:
      d:
          Child text.
          + {super.d}

  anchor DoublePlus extends Base:
      d:
          Child text.
          ++ {super.d}
  ```

  `Plus.d` is `"Child text.Base text."` and `DoublePlus.d` is
  `"Child text.\nBase text."`.
- A block holding only `+ {x}` is the same as `{x}`.
- To put inherited prose in front with a space, interpolate instead:
  `${super.description} and more from the child.`

## 6. Expressions

**Nothing is evaluated unless it is in braces.** `a + b` is the string
`"a + b"`, and `{a + b}` is `3` when `a` is 1 and `b` is 2. The braces keep the
compiler simple, and they mean an unrecognized word never silently falls back
to being a string.

- Inside the braces, **bare words are symbols**. Quote string operands:
  `{2 + "Hello"}` gives `"2Hello"`. An unknown name is `unresolved-symbol`.
  List literals inside braces follow the same rule: `{["A", "B"] + ["C"]}`.
- **Keep the whole expression inside the braces.** `{this.flag && false}`
  evaluates; `{this.flag} && false` is text around an expression.
- **Braces that don't hold a valid expression are an error**, and so is an
  empty `{}` or `${}`. To write braces as text, escape them: `\ {1 +} \`.
- **Forward references resolve.** Unresolved references are errors, and so are
  cyclic values: `A: {B}` together with `B: {A}` fails with `cyclic-value`.
- Collections are copied by value:

  ```piton
  myList: [1, 2, 3]
  myDictionary:
      list: {myList}
  newList: {myDictionary.list + [4, 5, 6]}
  ```

  `newList` is `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]`.
- **Anchors are copied too, but the copy still knows which anchor it is.** If
  `x` is `{Foo}`, then `{x == Foo}` is `true`, `${x}` is `"Foo"`, and `x`
  passes a `Foo` type constraint. The output is still a copy of Foo's content.
  For a link instead of a copy, use `@{Foo}`.

### 6.1 The four expression forms

| Form | Name | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `{expr}` | Standard | The intrinsic value with its type preserved. An anchor serializes as its resolved content (a copy that keeps its identity). |
| `${expr}` | String | Converts the result to a string. |
| `#{expr}` | Numeric | Converts the result to a number. |
| `@{expr}` | Reference | A reference to an anchor or a property on one. Renders as a link or path, never as the content. |

Use `@{X}` to point at another document, `{X}` to embed a copy of it, and
`${X}` to mention it by name.

### 6.2 Expressions in text

If the whole value is one expression (`total: {a + b}`), it keeps its type. If
there is other text around it:

- `${x}` turns the result into a string, so the whole value is a string.
- `{x}` with a simple value drops it into the text: `Total: {a + b}` is
  `"Total: 3"`.
- `{x}` with a list, dictionary or anchor copies it in and **turns the
  property into an implicit list**. `See {Foo} for details` becomes a list of
  `"See"`, a copy of Foo, and `"for details"`.
- `@{x}` puts in a reference, which ends up as a link or a path.

### 6.3 Conversions

`${}` (string):

- A string is returned unchanged. A number becomes its text form. A boolean
  becomes `true` or `false`. Null becomes `null`.
- An anchor becomes its name as written in the source: `${Child}` gives
  `"Child"`, and `${self}` gives the name of the current most-derived anchor.
  It is not turned into a title.
- A named list or dictionary becomes its name: `Anchor.propertyName`, or just
  the variable name at the top of a file. So if `tags` is a top-level list,
  `${tags}` is `"tags"`.
- A list or dictionary with no name (`${[1, 2]}`) is `no-string-form`.
- **`${}` never pulls in the contents** of a list, dictionary or anchor, only

  ```piton

      version:: string: 1.0

  export byValue: Information about Piton {Metadata}
  export byLink: Information about Piton @{Metadata}
  ```

  `byName` is `"Information about Piton Metadata"`, `byValue` is
  `["Information about Piton", {"name": "Piton", "version": "1.0"}]`, and
  `byLink` is `"Information about Piton ./Metadata.json:Metadata"` (in
  Markdown, `[Metadata](./Metadata.md#metadata)`).

- In structured output the value stays a string; whatever escaping the output
  format needs is applied when it is serialized.

`#{}` (numeric):

- A number is returned unchanged. A string converts only if the **entire**

- Booleans, null, collections and anchors are rejected (`not-a-number`).
- The result is a number you can keep computing with. In structured output it
  stays numeric; it becomes text only when the output format needs text.

| Group | Operators | Rules |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Access | `.` | Property access on dictionaries and anchors. |
| Arithmetic | `+ - * / %` | Numbers only. Division or modulo by zero is an error. `%` keeps the sign of the left side: `{-7 % 3}` is `-1`. |
| Comparison | `== != < <= > >=` | The result is a boolean. `==` and `!=` work on every type (see below). `< <= > >=` work on numbers and on strings (by Unicode code point); anything else, or a number against a string, is an error. |

# How Suspense works

Suspense is an application for working on a project whose spec, written in Piton, describes its code. The user sends you prompts from it in one of five modes:

- Code changes the code and leaves the spec as it is.
- Chain changes the spec, then the code to match it.
- Spec changes the spec and leaves the code as it is.
- Ask asks a question and changes nothing.
- Freeform passes a prompt to you exactly as typed.

Code, Chain, Spec, and Freeform prompts are tasks. Tasks run in two lanes, a spec lane and a code lane, one task at a time in each; a task waits in the queue behind the tasks of its own lane. Questions from Ask run at once and never queue.

A Chain prompt runs as two steps, each its own run in its own lane. The spec step writes the prompt into the spec. Once the spec is built, the code step is sent the same prompt and what the spec step replied, and changes the code to match the spec as built.

Suspense adds each mode's instructions to a prompt itself, in a block marked <task-instructions> at its head, together with the spec's references and the task's understanding file. So a prompt written for a mode is only what the user wants done, in the user's own terms. Never put a <task-instructions> block in a prompt you write, nor steps the mode already takes, nor instructions about building, checking, or the understanding file.

To write a good prompt for each mode:

- A Chain or Spec prompt says what should be true of the application once it is met, not how to edit the spec.
- A Code prompt says what the code should do, and may link to the compiled reference for the part of the spec it follows.
- An Ask prompt is a question.
- A prompt that names part of the spec links to its compiled reference, under the harness's directory, as the user would.

An answer hands a prompt back to the user as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-prompt` and the mode it is for, such as ```` ```suspense-prompt chain ````, holding only the prompt's text. It asks the user something back as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-question`: the question first, then any answers to pick from, one per line, each starting with `- `. Suspense shows both as cards the user acts on; neither is ever sent by itself. A prompt card has buttons that send it to Code, Chain, or Spec, whichever mode it names, and one that puts it in the chat input to edit first.

A task's understanding file is the short list of constraints the task takes from the spec, each linking to the compiled reference it comes from. Suspense shows it beside the task as it runs.

The user can cancel a task, resend it, send it to the other mode, send more to a task while it runs, and start a new conversation. A prompt never needs to say that any of this is possible.

### Items

## Creating

Creating a story is quick, as adding a card is in Trello and adding an issue is in Linear: a story is added in the list it belongs in, right where it will sit. Sending the sprint moves its stories into the "Current sprint" column, to the right of Next sprint, so Next sprint is empty again and stories added meanwhile go there, to be the sprint after. Current sprint and Done are columns of the board whatever they hold, never appearing, disappearing, or collapsing; while no sprint is under way Current sprint is empty and shows its empty state, as Done does before anything is done. A story in Current sprint keeps its place, its card showing its task's status as it queues, runs, and ends, and clicking it opens its task in the Tasks tab; it can't be moved or edited there. Once every story of Current sprint has ended, its column's heading offers "Close sprint", which moves the stories that are done into the Done column, their cards muted, and those that failed, were cancelled, or stopped to the start of Next sprint, in their order, to be sent again. While a sprint is current, Send sprint is disabled, its tooltip saying a sprint is already under way.
Send sprint only ever moves into Current sprint the stories it actually sent. A story with nothing to send, its title and its prompt both empty, is skipped: it stays in Next sprint, where it was, and Send sprint's result says, muted, how many it skipped and why, as "1 empty story left in Next sprint". A sprint where every story is empty sends nothing and makes no Current sprint.
Once a sprint is done, it can always be closed. Every story of Current sprint counts as ended once its task has ended, done, failed, cancelled, or stopped, or once its task can no longer be found, as when its record was deleted, it was never recorded, or the application quit before it was. A story whose task is missing is never shown as Queued, or as anything still to come: its card reads "Task missing", muted, in the theme's warning colour, its tooltip saying its task can't be found, and it counts as ended and not Done. A story still waiting in its lane's queue, or held for review, as the paused section says, is still to come and hasn't ended. So Close sprint shows as soon as no story of Current sprint is building, compiling, running, paused, queued, or held, and never waits on a task that can't arrive.
Close sprint treats a story whose task is missing as it treats one that failed or was cancelled: it goes back to the start of Next sprint, with the others sent again, in their order, never into Done. Closing saves the sections, Done, Next sprint, the Backlog, Draft, and the emptied Current sprint, to `order.json` straight away, as the [ProjectData](../project-data/index.md#project-data) says, and Current sprint's state is worked out afresh from the stories' tasks whenever the plan is read, so a sprint that finished, or whose tasks went missing, before a reload or a restart can still be closed after it, as before.

Dragging a card on the board feels as it does in Trello, and the board opens the gap, as the [DragReorderBehaviour](../../ui/behaviours/drag-reorder/index.md#drag-reorder-behaviour) lets its user do, in place of the accent line alone. Only the board's cards move this way; steps in an open story, and every other list, are dragged as the [DragReorderBehaviour](../../ui/behaviours/drag-reorder/index.md#drag-reorder-behaviour) says, with its line.
A card picked up by its grip lifts off the board as a full-size copy of itself, the same width and height, drawn as the parts draw a story card, tilted a few degrees, about 3, on the theme's overlay surface with its edge border and the soft shadow the [Theme](../../ui/theme/index.md#theme)'s elevation gives floating surfaces, the one shadow on the board. It follows the pointer, held where it was grabbed, and never takes the mouse. The card's own place in its column becomes the gap it left, empty, the card's height, so the column doesn't jump as it lifts.
Where the card would land, the cards slide apart to open a placeholder the dragged card's height, 8 pixels from the cards either side, as the cards are spaced: a box the card's size on the theme's well surface, with its corners rounded 6 pixels as a card's are, and no border, so it reads as an empty slot. The gap is chosen as the [DragReorderBehaviour](../../ui/behaviours/drag-reorder/index.md#drag-reorder-behaviour) chooses it, among the cards of the column the pointer is over, and only one is open at a time: as the pointer moves into another gap, or another column, the gap it left closes as the new one opens, and the gap the card came from closes once the pointer leaves its column, opening again if it comes back. A column that takes no drops opens no gap, and its cards never move while a card is dragged over it.
Nothing waits on motion while the user is waiting on it. The gap the card would drop into is updated at once, the moment the pointer crosses the middle of a card, exactly as the [DragReorderBehaviour](../../ui/behaviours/drag-reorder/index.md#drag-reorder-behaviour) says, and a drop always goes where the gap was chosen, even while the cards are still sliding toward it; only the sliding of the cards around it is animated, quickly, as below.
Dropped over an open gap, the copy settles into it: it straightens, its shadow fades, and it moves from where it was released into the placeholder, which it then is, the story saved in its new place at the moment of the drop, as every change to the plan is. Dropped anywhere else, or where it began, it settles back into the gap it came from the same way, and nothing changes. Escape while dragging cancels it, settling the card back where it was.
A card moved any other way animates to its new place, as Linear's do, in a quick motion of about 150 milliseconds, eased out, sliding from where it was to where it now is, the cards it passes or leaves sliding to close and open the room it takes, never fading or bouncing. That covers every move the sprint describes: "Move to next sprint", "Move to backlog", and "Move to draft" from a card's menu, or the bulk bar, Alt+Up, Alt+Down, Alt+Left, and Alt+Right, Ctrl+Enter, Send sprint moving its stories into Current sprint, and Close sprint moving them into Done and back to the start of Next sprint. A card added, as by a composer or Duplicate, slides the cards below it down to make room, and a card deleted slides them up to close it, in the same motion. The board scrolls sideways, and a column up or down, to keep a moved card that has focus in view, as the keyboard says. Focus goes with the card at once, not when its motion ends, and the plan is saved at once.
The side panel slides in from the board's right as it opens, in the same quick motion, the board narrowing alongside it, and slides back out to the right as it closes, the board widening as it goes; replacing what it holds with another story, drafting, or research changes its content in place, with no slide. Its content, and focus in it, are there as soon as it starts to open.
The open story's card is kept in view, however the board changes around it. As the side panel opens and the board narrows, the board scrolls sideways alongside it, in the same quick motion, just enough to keep the open story's card fully in view, when it was fully in view before; a card already partly out of view is left where it is. A story opened from anywhere outside the board, as a proposal's "Added to Backlog" or "Added to <story>" link, or a palette or ribbon action that opens one, scrolls the board sideways and its column up or down, in the same motion, just enough that its card is fully in view, then highlights it as the open story. Clicking a card only partly in view opens it and scrolls the board and its column just enough to show it all; a card already fully in view never scrolls anything. Each scroll moves only as far as it must, the card landing at the nearest edge of the view, never centred.
Nothing above the view moves what is in it. In a column scrolled away from its top, a card above the view that is added, deleted, or changes height, as a story's status or step lines arriving in Current sprint, or a sprint closing and its stories leaving, never moves the cards in view: the column's scroll shifts by the same amount, at once and with no motion, so they stay exactly where they were, and the column's thumb moves without jumping, as the [Scrollbar.steadiness](../../ui/components/scrollbar/index.md#steadiness) says. A column at its top keeps its top, and cards in view move as the motion above says.
Every motion here takes about 150 milliseconds, never longer, and a move made while another is still under way starts from wherever the card is then, never queued behind it.

## Auto Start

Next sprint can start on its own: a "Start automatically" switch on Next sprint's heading, beside Send sprint, its tooltip saying the next sprint starts as soon as the current one is done. It starts off, and is saved with the plan, in `order.json`, so it is kept across reloads and restarts.
While it is on, once every story of Current sprint has ended Done, the current sprint closes by itself, as Close sprint closes it, and Next sprint, if it holds a story, is sent at once, as Send sprint sends it, with nobody having to start it; and while no sprint is current, a story added to an empty Next sprint starts it the same way. A sprint that ended with a story failed, cancelled, stopped, or with its task missing, never starts the next by itself: it waits, Close sprint offered as ever, and the switch's row says, in the theme's warning colour, why the next didn't start. Nor does the next start while planning is paused, as the paused section says: it starts once the pause is ended by Resume, or Approve, if the switch is still on. An empty Next sprint starts nothing.
Each time a sprint starts by itself, a passive notification says so, "Next sprint started: 4 stories", with a link that opens Planning, and the debug log records it. Turning the switch off never stops a sprint already sent; it only keeps the next from starting by itself. Turning it on while no sprint is current and Next sprint holds a story starts Next sprint at once, as adding a story to it would, unless planning is paused.
The switch works while Planning isn't open, from the plan as saved, whichever tab is shown. When the project is opened, or the application starts, with the switch on, no sprint current, and Next sprint holding a story, it doesn't start by itself; the switch's row says, muted, "Waiting to start", with a "Start now" button, so a sprint never begins unseen as the application opens. A current sprint whose stories were cut off when the application quit, as every run is, ended them, and never starts the next by itself.
While the switch is on, Next sprint's heading shows "Auto" beside its count, in the theme's accent, and the ribbon's Send Sprint button's tooltip says the next sprint starts automatically.

The stories, their order, and which section each is in are saved with the project's data, as the [ProjectData](../project-data/index.md#project-data) says, in `.suspense/planning/`, a file per story, holding its hidden anchor as a queued prompt's is, and an `order.json` listing the sections, Draft, the Backlog, Next sprint, Current sprint, and Done, and their stories in order, so the plan is kept with the project and comes back as it was left. A plan saved before Draft existed, its `order.json` with no Draft section, loads as it was with Draft empty, and is saved with one the next time the plan is. A story's steps are saved in its own file, in their order, as its steps say, never apart from it.

## Steps

A story can have steps: one or more further prompts, each a piece of the story done after the one before, as a chain's steps are. Each step has a prompt, a mode of its own, Code or Spec, starting as the story's, and a model and effort, starting as the story's, and may have attachments. A story with no steps is just its own prompt, as before; its prompt is always its first step.
An open story lists its steps beneath its prompt, in order, each a row numbered from 2, the story's own prompt being 1, with its mode pill and the first line of its prompt, opening in place to edit, as a story does. "Add step", beneath the last, adds one at the end, open and focused; several can be added one after another, Enter in an empty step's prompt adding none. Steps are reordered by dragging, as the [DragReorderBehaviour](../../ui/behaviours/drag-reorder/index.md#drag-reorder-behaviour) says, or Alt+Up and Alt+Down, and each has a remove button in its row and in its menu. The story's own prompt stays first and can't be moved among them.
A step belongs to its story and to nothing else. It is saved in the story's file, in a `steps` list of the story's hidden anchor, in its order, and saved as every change to the plan is, straight away; a story duplicated copies its steps, and one deleted deletes them. Its order is kept wherever the story goes, between sections, into a sprint, and back from Done.

The same steps, in the same order, are what every place shows, since every place reads them from the story's own file.
A step is only ever added to a story that exists. It says so in plain words where it was asked for, as "That story no longer exists, so the step wasn't added", in the theme's error colour, as the states say, with what was to be added kept, so it can be added to another story or as a new one. A step added to a story already sent is refused the same way, saying the story has been sent.

## Layout

Everything in Planning is laid out on one rhythm, so the board scans at a glance. The board fills the body beneath the tab bar, with 24 pixels of padding at its top, sides, and foot. Its columns are all the same fixed width, 320 pixels, 16 pixels apart, each as tall as the board, set side by side from its left edge in the order work moves, Draft, the first, Backlog, Next sprint, Current sprint, Done, and Findings, the last. Each column is a list, as Trello draws one: a container of its own, as the parts draw a list, on the theme's recessed surface, one step from the base the board is on, its corners rounded 8 pixels, with its heading and its cards inside it, and no border. Three things set a list apart from the board's base, all quieter than any card's state: its recessed surface; the theme's pressed bevel around it, inside its rounded corners, so it reads as sunk into the base; and the 16 pixel gaps between columns. Each column also has a look of its own, telling it from its neighbours: a 2 pixel edge along the list's top, inside its rounded corners and above its heading, in the colour its status icon uses, as the parts give it, laid over the recessed surface at 50%, so Draft's is tertiary text, as the Backlog's is, the two told apart by their icons, Next sprint's secondary text, Current sprint's the accent, Done's success, and Findings' secondary text. The edge is the only place a column's colour shows besides its icon: its heading, its name, its cards, its empty state, and the drag placeholder keep their own surfaces and colours untouched, the placeholder its well surface. Laid over at half strength and 2 pixels tall, a column's edge is always quieter than a card's hover, its selected surface, its focus ring, or the open story's 3 pixel accent line, as the Theme's hierarchy orders decoration below state.
Each column's heading reads as Linear heads a group: a row 32 pixels tall at the list's top, holding, from its left, the column's status icon, 14 pixels, as the parts give it; its name in small semibold text, in the theme's primary text colour; its count beside it, muted; and its actions at its right, each a labelled button, never an icon alone, as the sections give them: "Draft stories" and "Research" on the Backlog; "Send sprint" and "Start automatically" on Next sprint; "Close sprint" on Current sprint, once its sprint can close. A heading with more actions than fit its width wraps them onto a second line beneath its name rather than cutting any off; Draft's heading has no actions but its "+ Add". On Draft, the Backlog, and Next sprint, hovering the heading, or focus anywhere in it, shows "+ Add" just after its count, a small ghost button with a plus icon and its label, never the icon alone, its tooltip saying it adds a story at the top of the list; it takes its room in the heading whether shown or not, so the heading's actions never shift as it appears, and the other columns' headings have none. 8 pixels beneath the heading come its cards, one beneath another, 8 pixels apart, each the list's full inner width.

It scrolls with the cards, after the last of them. Current sprint, Done, and Findings have no "Add story" line.

78:Wherever the story is shown, its steps are too: its card in Planning shows how many beneath its title, muted, as "3 steps", with the list in its tooltip; the open story lists them as above; a proposal to add to it shows them, so what it would add to can be seen; and once it is sent, it is sent as a chain, its prompt first and each step after it in order, each step sent only once the one before it finishes, as the [PromptEditor](../prompt-mode/index.md#prompt-editor)'s chained tasks are, so the Tasks tab shows the story as one chain with its steps beneath it. A story sent can't be given more steps; its steps, sent or still to come, read as they were sent. In Current sprint, a story with steps lists its steps on its card, beneath its title, a line for each step, in order, each with its number, the first line of its prompt cut off with an ellipsis, and its own status, as a running chain's are in the Tasks tab; in Done, and in a finding started from the story, its steps are listed the same way, collapsed to its step count until it is expanded. The same steps, in the same order, are what every place shows, since every place reads them from the story's own file.
79:A step is only ever added to a story that exists. Adding one to a story that doesn't, as one deleted while a proposal naming it waited, or by another window, or whose file was removed from `.suspense/planning/` meanwhile, changes nothing: no story is made for it, no other story is given it, and nothing is saved. It says so in plain words where it was asked for, as "That story no longer exists, so the step wasn't added", in the theme's error colour, as the states say, with what was to be added kept, so it can be added to another story or as a new one. A step added to a story already sent is refused the same way, saying the story has been sent.
83:Everything in Planning is laid out on one rhythm, so the board scans at a glance. The board fills the body beneath the tab bar, with 24 pixels of padding at its top, sides, and foot. Its columns are all the same fixed width, 320 pixels, 16 pixels apart, each as tall as the board, set side by side from its left edge in the order work moves, Draft, the first, Backlog, Next sprint, Current sprint, Done, and Findings, the last. Each column is a list, as Trello draws one: a container of its own, as the parts draw a list, on the theme's recessed surface, one step from the base the board is on, its corners rounded 8 pixels, with its heading and its cards inside it, and no border. Three things set a list apart from the board's base, all quieter than any card's state: its recessed surface; the theme's pressed bevel around it, inside its rounded corners, so it reads as sunk into the base; and the 16 pixel gaps between columns. Each column also has a look of its own, telling it from its neighbours: a 2 pixel edge along the list's top, inside its rounded corners and above its heading, in the colour its status icon uses, as the parts give it, laid over the recessed surface at 50%, so Draft's is tertiary text, as the Backlog's is, the two told apart by their icons, Next sprint's secondary text, Current sprint's the accent, Done's success, and Findings' secondary text. The edge is the only place a column's colour shows besides its icon: its heading, its name, its cards, its empty state, and the drag placeholder keep their own surfaces and colours untouched, the placeholder its well surface. Laid over at half strength and 2 pixels tall, a column's edge is always quieter than a card's hover, its selected surface, its focus ring, or the open story's 3 pixel accent line, as the Theme's hierarchy orders decoration below state.
84:Each column's heading reads as Linear heads a group: a row 32 pixels tall at the list's top, holding, from its left, the column's status icon, 14 pixels, as the parts give it; its name in small semibold text, in the theme's primary text colour; its count beside it, muted; and its actions at its right, each a labelled button, never an icon alone, as the sections give them: "Draft stories" and "Research" on the Backlog; "Send sprint" and "Start automatically" on Next sprint; "Close sprint" on Current sprint, once its sprint can close. A heading with more actions than fit its width wraps them onto a second line beneath its name rather than cutting any off; Draft's heading has no actions but its "+ Add". On Draft, the Backlog, and Next sprint, hovering the heading, or focus anywhere in it, shows "+ Add" just after its count, a small ghost button with a plus icon and its label, never the icon alone, its tooltip saying it adds a story at the top of the list; it takes its room in the heading whether shown or not, so the heading's actions never shift as it appears, and the other columns' headings have none. 8 pixels beneath the heading come its cards, one beneath another, 8 pixels apart, each the list's full inner width.
88:The side panel is the one place anything opens: an open story, Draft stories, and Research, never beneath a heading or a card, and never in a popup or over the board. A composer is not an opened story but a card being written, and is the one thing drawn in a list, where its story will sit. It is docked at the right of Planning's tab, 400 pixels wide, as tall as the tab, from the tab bar down to the bottom of the body, a 1 pixel line in the theme's line colour along its left edge, and it scrolls up and down on its own, its heading staying at its top, with the [Scrollbar](../../ui/components/scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar) along its right while it holds more than fits. Only one thing is in it at a time: opening a story, drafting, or research replaces whatever it held, and closing it leaves nothing there. While it is open the board narrows to the space left of it, its columns keeping their width and scrolling sideways as ever when they no longer fit; the panel never covers the board, and the board never covers it. Closed, it takes no space and the board fills the tab again. It slides in and out at the right, as motion says.
89:While paused, the pause bar runs across the top of the whole board, above every column, as the paused section says, beside the side panel when it is open, never over it. Each column is headed as above, so nothing sits outside the rhythm, and an open story, a drafting or research panel, and the citations and steps inside a story all use the same five parts, below.

100:Stories are selected as Linear selects issues, to be acted on together. Ctrl+click (Cmd+click on macOS) on a card toggles it alone in or out of the selection, the rest kept; Shift+click selects the range within its column from the card last clicked or toggled there to the clicked one, inclusive, added to the selection, or the clicked card alone when nothing in that column was clicked or toggled yet; and X toggles one from the keyboard, as the keyboard says. A selection can hold stories from all three lists at once. A plain click opens the story in the side panel as ever, and leaves the selection as it is. Selected cards show the theme's selected surface, as the story card above says, distinct from focus and from the open story's line. The selection is the board's own, never saved with the plan: a selected story leaves it when it is deleted or leaves Draft, the Backlog, and Next sprint, as when the sprint it is in is sent.
101:While any card is selected, the bulk bar runs across the board's foot, beneath its columns, beside the side panel when it is open, never over it nor over the board: a row 40 pixels tall, on the theme's raised surface with a 1 pixel line in the theme's line colour along its top, the columns shortening to make room as it slides up in motion's quick motion, and lengthening again as it slides away once nothing is selected. At its left it names how many are selected, as "3 selected"; at its right, labelled buttons, never icons alone, in this order: "Move to next sprint", which moves the selected stories in the Backlog to the end of Next sprint; "Move to backlog", which moves those in Draft and in Next sprint to the end of the Backlog; "Move to draft", which moves those in the Backlog to the end of Draft; "Draft with agent", which drafts each selected story in a run of its own, all at once, as drafting with the agent says; "Change mode", which opens a mode picker above it, the one a card's pill opens, setting the mode of every selected story to the one picked, their steps keeping their own; "Duplicate", which duplicates each, every copy just beneath its original, as a card's menu does; "Delete", which deletes them all after one confirmation naming how many, as "Delete 3 stories?"; and "Clear", which empties the selection. Every move keeps the stories' order, as the selection orders them, Draft's first, top to bottom, then the Backlog's, then Next sprint's, and animates as motion says; a move button is disabled, its tooltip saying why, while none of the selection is in the list it moves from. Moved stories stay selected, duplicates are not selected, and the originals stay so. The bar has no Send and sends nothing: a story still reaches work only through the sprint, as the sprint says.
124:A draft about a story, from "Ask agent" or "Draft with agent", may propose rewriting it: a proposal whose target is the story itself, to be rewritten, its title, prompt, mode, and spec citations replaced by the proposal's, its steps and attachments kept; as well as additions to it, each a step, as the proposals say. Where a story holds more than one piece of work, the draft splits it: the story's rewrite comes first, the first piece, with its steps, and each other piece is a proposal for a new story of its own, its target "New story", with its own title, prompt, mode, and spec citations, grounded as the spec grounding says. A story that is one piece of work gets only its rewrite and its steps, and no new story.
130:Each story drafts as "Ask agent" drafts an open story, with no request box and nothing to type: the run is told the story's title, its prompt, its mode, and its steps, and asked to turn it into a full story, a fuller prompt, the mode that fits it, the steps it needs, and its spec citations, grounded as the spec grounding says; and, where the story holds more than one piece of work, to split it, as drafting says: the story's rewrite, the first piece, with its steps, then a "New story" proposal for each other piece, each with its own title, prompt, mode, and spec citations, grounded the same way. A story that is one piece of work gets only its rewrite and its steps. Each run is its own, in a run of its own with no session, a Question run as the proposals say, with the planning prompt of the [BakedSystemPrompts](../harness-integration/baked-prompts/index.md#baked-system-prompts). All the runs start at once, none waiting on another, however many stories are drafted; one ending, failing, or being stopped never touches the others. A story already drafting is skipped, so drafting it again starts no second run.
133:A story's waiting proposals are kept until each is decided, saved with the plan as soon as its run ends, in `.suspense/planning/proposals/`, a file per story named by its id, so they come back, and its card's count with them, after closing Planning, a reload, or a restart. A story deleted takes its waiting proposals with it, and one duplicated copies none.
134:Nothing reaches the plan until it is accepted, as the proposals say. Accepting the story's rewrite rewrites it as proposed, and accepting an addition adds its step to the story's end, as the proposal cards say. Accepting a new story split off it adds that story at the end of the Backlog, marked "From agent", as the proposal cards say, never into Draft and never into Next sprint. A story in Draft whose rewrite or addition is accepted moves to the end of the Backlog, as "Move to backlog" moves it and motion animates it, staying open if it was; accepting a new story split off it never moves it, and a story in the Backlog or Next sprint stays where it is. A story sent while its proposals waited can no longer be rewritten or added to, as the proposal cards say.
159:The citations are shown on the proposal's card, beneath its prompt, as a short list, each element's name, as `Planning.sprint`, and its file, muted, as a link that opens that place in the Piton source, a "No match" entry muted with a small marker, and are kept with the story once it is accepted, listed in the open story beneath its steps as "Spec", and shown in its card's tooltip. They can be edited with the story, removed, or added to by hand: "Add citation" opens a picker of the spec's elements, its anchors and their properties, found from the Piton source and searched by name, never from the compiled reference, and adds the one picked in the same form, checked as a proposal's are.

content.text: Reading the Planning reference's Steps, Drafting, and Proposals sections now.

content.content:
## Steps

A story can have steps: one or more further prompts, each a piece of the story done after the one before, as a chain's steps are. Each step has a prompt, a mode of its own, Code or Spec, starting as the story's, and a model and effort, starting as the story's, and may have attachments. A story with no steps is just its own prompt, as before; its prompt is always its first step.
An open story lists its steps beneath its prompt, in order, each a row numbered from 2, the story's own prompt being 1, with its mode pill and the first line of its prompt, opening in place to edit, as a story does. "Add step", beneath the last, adds one at the end, open and focused; several can be added one after another, Enter in an empty step's prompt adding none. Steps are reordered by dragging, as the [DragReorderBehaviour](../../ui/behaviours/drag-reorder/index.md#drag-reorder-behaviour) says, or Alt+Up and Alt+Down, and each has a remove button in its row and in its menu. The story's own prompt stays first and can't be moved among them.
A step belongs to its story and to nothing else. It is saved in the story's file, in a `steps` list of the story's hidden anchor, in its order, and saved as every change to the plan is, straight away; a story duplicated copies its steps, and one deleted deletes them. Its order is kept wherever the story goes, between sections, into a sprint, and back from Done.
Wherever the story is shown, its steps are too: its card in Planning shows how many beneath its title, muted, as "3 steps", with the list in its tooltip; the open story lists them as above; a proposal to add to it shows them, so what it would add to can be seen; and once it is sent, it is sent as a chain, its prompt first and each step after it in order, each step sent only once the one before it finishes, as the [PromptEditor](../prompt-mode/index.md#prompt-editor)'s chained tasks are, so the Tasks tab shows the story as one chain with its steps beneath it. A story sent can't be given more steps; its steps, sent or still to come, read as they were sent. In Current sprint, a story with steps lists its steps on its card, beneath its title, a line for each step, in order, each with its number, the first line of its prompt cut off with an ellipsis, and its own status, as a running chain's are in the Tasks tab; in Done, and in a finding started from the story, its steps are listed the same way, collapsed to its step count until it is expanded. The same steps, in the same order, are what every place shows, since every place reads them from the story's own file.
A step is only ever added to a story that exists. Adding one to a story that doesn't, as one deleted while a proposal naming it waited, or by another window, or whose file was removed from `.suspense/planning/` meanwhile, changes nothing: no story is made for it, no other story is given it, and nothing is saved. It says so in plain words where it was asked for, as "That story no longer exists, so the step wasn't added", in the theme's error colour, as the states say, with what was to be added kept, so it can be added to another story or as a new one. A step added to a story already sent is refused the same way, saying the story has been sent.

## Drafting

Drafting stories shows its work in one place, the side panel, docked at the board's right, as the layout places it, replacing whatever it held, never in a popup that hides the list. It has the request box at its top, labelled "Describe what you want", and beneath it, while the run goes, its research: a muted line of what the harness is doing, as "Reading the spec…", with its spinner, updating as it goes, and a "Stop" button. Once it ends, the panel lists its proposals, as below, then "Accept all" and "Reject all" buttons along the panel's foot, and closes itself once none is left to decide. A run that fails shows its error, as the states say, and leaves the request in its box to try again; one that proposes nothing says so, as an empty state. Proposals are kept until each is decided, so closing Planning and coming back finds them as they were.
Drafting can also be started from an open story, with "Ask agent" in its card's menu or the open story's footer: the request box then reads "What does this story need?", the run is told the story's title and prompt, and the drafting panel takes the open story's place in the side panel, the story's card staying highlighted while the draft is about it.
A draft about a story, from "Ask agent" or "Draft with agent", may propose rewriting it: a proposal whose target is the story itself, to be rewritten, its title, prompt, mode, and spec citations replaced by the proposal's, its steps and attachments kept; as well as additions to it, each a step, as the proposals say. Where a story holds more than one piece of work, the draft splits it: the story's rewrite comes first, the first piece, with its steps, and each other piece is a proposal for a new story of its own, its target "New story", with its own title, prompt, mode, and spec citations, grounded as the spec grounding says. A story that is one piece of work gets only its rewrite and its steps, and no new story.
The request is sent with the panel's "Draft" button, its primary action, or by pressing Enter in the request box, whichever label it reads; Ctrl+Enter there starts it too, and the button's tooltip gives Enter as its shortcut. Shift+Enter adds a new line in the box and sends nothing. A request that is empty, or only spaces and new lines, starts nothing, and the button is disabled while it is. While a run is going, Enter starts no second one, and the button is disabled. Enter in the request box only ever sends the request: the list's Enter, opening or closing the focused story, never fires while focus is in the box.

## Drafting With Agent

Several stories can be drafted at once, each in a run of its own. "Draft with agent" is an item of the menu of every card in Draft, the Backlog, and Next sprint, the menu its hover button opens and right-clicking opens at the pointer, as the parts say, and a button of the bulk bar, drafting every selected story; a card in Current sprint or Done, and a finding, has no such item. It is meant mainly for Draft's rough stories, but drafts any story it is offered on.
Each story drafts as "Ask agent" drafts an open story, with no request box and nothing to type: the run is told the story's title, its prompt, its mode, and its steps, and asked to turn it into a full story, a fuller prompt, the mode that fits it, the steps it needs, and its spec citations, grounded as the spec grounding says; and, where the story holds more than one piece of work, to split it, as drafting says: the story's rewrite, the first piece, with its steps, then a "New story" proposal for each other piece, each with its own title, prompt, mode, and spec citations, grounded the same way. A story that is one piece of work gets only its rewrite and its steps. Each run is its own, in a run of its own with no session, a Question run as the proposals say, with the planning prompt of the [BakedSystemPrompts](../harness-integration/baked-prompts/index.md#baked-system-prompts). All the runs start at once, none waiting on another, however many stories are drafted; one ending, failing, or being stopped never touches the others. A story already drafting is skipped, so drafting it again starts no second run.
The drafts never take over the side panel, which holds only one thing at a time, as the layout says: a story drafting this way shows its run on its own card, and opening the story while it drafts shows the story in the panel as ever, its run going on. While its run goes, the card's property row shows the loading state, as the states say, "Drafting…" with its spinner, in place of its status, and its menu has "Stop", which stops that run alone and keeps whatever it had proposed by then, in place of "Draft with agent". A run that fails shows its error on that card, beneath its property row, as the states say, in the theme's error colour with "Details" collapsed and "Try again", which drafts the story again; the error stays until the story is drafted again or opened. A run cut off when the application quits, as every run is, shows the same error once it is open again.
When a run ends, its card's property row shows how many of its proposals are waiting, as "3 proposals", in the theme's accent, or "1 proposal", counting down as each is decided and gone once none is left, counting every kind: its rewrite, its additions, and its new stories; a run that proposed nothing shows "Nothing proposed", muted, until the story is next opened. Opening the story shows them all in the side panel, beneath the story's own fields, under a "Proposals" heading, as proposal cards, as the proposal cards say, each new story's card labelled "New story", in the order the run gave them, its rewrite first, then its new stories and additions in the order given, with "Accept all" and "Reject all" beneath the last; "Accept all" accepts the rewrite, every addition, and every new story together. Drafting a story again while proposals of its wait adds the new ones after them.
A story's waiting proposals are kept until each is decided, saved with the plan as soon as its run ends, in `.suspense/planning/proposals/`, a file per story named by its id, so they come back, and its card's count with them, after closing Planning, a reload, or a restart. A story deleted takes its waiting proposals with it, and one duplicated copies none.
Nothing reaches the plan until it is accepted, as the proposals say. Accepting the story's rewrite rewrites it as proposed, and accepting an addition adds its step to the story's end, as the proposal cards say. Accepting a new story split off it adds that story at the end of the Backlog, marked "From agent", as the proposal cards say, never into Draft and never into Next sprint. A story in Draft whose rewrite or addition is accepted moves to the end of the Backlog, as "Move to backlog" moves it and motion animates it, staying open if it was; accepting a new story split off it never moves it, and a story in the Backlog or Next sprint stays where it is. A story sent while its proposals waited can no longer be rewritten or added to, as the proposal cards say.

## Proposals

The agent never writes the plan itself. Its run is a Question run, as the [Sandbox](../sandbox/index.md#sandbox) says, able to read the project and change nothing, and Suspense data is never granted to it, so it can't touch `.suspense/planning/`; it only proposes, and nothing it proposes reaches the plan until the user accepts it.
Each proposal is one concrete task, with a title, a prompt, and the mode that fits it, and says where it should go: either "New story", to become a story of its own, or "Add to" a story, naming an existing story the run was shown, the open story first, to be added to it, or, in a draft about a story, "Rewrite", the story itself rewritten, as drafting says. The planning prompt of the [BakedSystemPrompts](../harness-integration/baked-prompts/index.md#baked-system-prompts) asks for each proposal as a fenced block whose info string is `suspense-story`, holding its title, its mode, its target, `new`, the story's id, or `rewrite`, its `spec` list of citations into the Piton source, as the spec grounding says, and its prompt, so the application reads it whatever else the reply says. The planning prompt explains the form with an example, as:
```suspense-story
title: Close a finished sprint
mode: chain
target: new
spec:
- spec/scope/planning/index.pi#Planning.sprint: when Close sprint shows
- No match: archiving a closed sprint
prompt:
Close sprint is offered once every story of the current sprint has
ended, as spec/scope/planning/index.pi#Planning.sprint says.
```
A block that names a story that no longer exists is shown as "New story", with a muted note saying so.

## Spec Grounding

A drafted story is grounded in the project's spec, never written from the request alone. Before proposing, the drafter searches the spec for what each story touches: the requirements and behaviours it changes or relies on, the names it uses, as a feature, a component, or a property, and the sections they are in. It reads the spec as every run does, from its compiled reference or from what `piton slice` prints, never from the Piton source, as the [ModeSystemPrompts](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/index.md#mode-system-prompts) says, and the planning prompt of the [BakedSystemPrompts](../harness-integration/baked-prompts/index.md#baked-system-prompts) tells it to.

content.content:
## Description

The prompts are Piton files in the repository's system-prompts folder, one for each piece of the application's own work.

## Prompts

- divergence.pi, for the two agents of a divergence analysis
- generate-skills.pi, for ranking the spec's scopes for skills
- rescope.pi, for finding concepts to extract into scopes, and for the refactoring prompt sent for those chosen
- run-targets.pi, for finding how the project is built, run, and tested
- commit-note.pi, for a finished task's commit note
- commit-message.pi, for writing a commit message
- file-search.pi, for the palette's search for a file by description
- prompt-title.pi, for titling a task or question so its hidden anchor can be named after it
- planning.pi, for breaking what is wanted into stories, each with a title, a prompt, a mode, and its spec citations as links into the Piton source, explained with an example, and for turning one story into a full story, proposing its rewrite and the steps it needs, as the Planning says
- research.pi, for a read-only investigation of a topic during planning, producing findings rather than changes, as the Planning says

## Writing

Each is an exported anchor, its text written as prose, one property for each paragraph or piece the application puts together, such as a heading above a list of files. What the application fills in is a name in angle brackets, such as <codeRoot>, so it isn't taken as Piton.

## Building

They are compiled with `piton compile` when the application is built, and built into it: changing one changes what the next build sends, and a prompt that doesn't compile fails the build, with piton's error. Each build keeps what it compiled in system-prompts/compiled.json, with the source, so the application still builds where `piton` isn't installed, such as on CI, from the prompts as last compiled, saying so.
